title: How GPS works
examples: How far away are the GPS satellites?
Does GPS use the internet to work?
What happens if one satellite stops working?

explain.say: Today we will learn how the Global Positioning System works. It helps us find our exact location anywhere on Earth.
First, we need satellites orbiting the Earth. These satellites send out radio signals constantly. They act like high-tech messengers in space.
Next, accurate timing is very important for GPS. The satellites must know the exact time they sent the signal. Time keeps the distance calculation correct.
The third step is called trilateration. This uses distances from three or more satellites. It pinpoints your position using geometry.
In real life, think about finding your school on a map. Your phone uses GPS signals from satellites to tell you exactly where you stand. It uses these steps all together.
A common mistake is forgetting that the signal travels at the speed of light. If timing is off by even a tiny bit, your location calculation will be wrong. Always remember the speed of light.

faq.q: Do all GPS satellites orbit the same way?
faq.a: No, they are placed in several orbital planes. This ensures coverage all over the globe. You might also ask: What are the GPS orbits like? Or: How are the satellites positioned?
asks: Are the satellites in a circle?
Do they all go around the Earth the same way?

faq.q: Does GPS rely on the internet to work?
faq.a: No, the basic positioning signal does not need the internet. The satellites send direct radio signals to your receiver. You might ask: Do I need Wi-Fi for GPS? Or: Is internet needed for location?
asks: Is it like using Google Maps online?
Does the signal need the web?

faq.q: How does trilateration actually calculate the spot?
faq.a: It calculates your position by finding the point where three spheres intersect. Each sphere represents the distance from one satellite. You might ask: What is the math behind this? Or: How do three signals meet?
asks: How many satellites are needed for a fix?

faq.q: What is the role of timing in GPS?
faq.a: Timing allows the receiver to calculate the distance accurately. The time difference tells us how far the signal has traveled. You might ask: Why is time so important? Or: How does time affect distance?
asks: What if the clock is wrong?

faq.q: Can GPS work underground or indoors?
faq.a: GPS signals are radio waves that can be blocked. Buildings and underground areas can weaken or block the signal. You might ask: Does concrete stop GPS? Or: Can I use GPS inside a building?

facts: GPS uses a constellation of satellites orbiting Earth.
The system requires precise time signals for accurate distance measurement.
Trilateration uses distances from at least three satellites to pinpoint a location.
The signals travel at the speed of light.

quiz.say: A phone needs signals from how many satellites for a basic location fix?
quiz.why: Three satellites allow the receiver to calculate the position using trilateration.

wrong.1: One satellite only tells you you are somewhere on a large sphere around it.
wrong.2: Two satellites only narrow your location down to a circle, not a point.
wrong.3: While four satellites can improve accuracy, three are the minimum required for the basic calculation.

quiz.say: What physical principle is essential for calculating distance in GPS?
quiz.why: The distance is calculated by multiplying the known speed of light by the measured time delay.

wrong.0: Sound travels much slower than light, so using this speed would give a wrong distance.
wrong.1: While similar, the speed of light is the precise constant used in these calculations.
wrong.2: The signal travels at the universal speed limit, which is the speed of light.

quiz.say: If the clock on the receiver is wrong, what happens to the location calculation?

options.show: The satellites will stop sending signals.
options.say: The satellites will stop sending signals.

options.show: The receiver will display an error message immediately.
options.say: The receiver will display an error message immediately.

options.show: The signal will be blocked by the Earth.
options.say: The signal will be blocked by the Earth.

options.show: The calculated distance will be incorrect.
options.say: The calculated distance will be incorrect.

quiz.why: Since distance depends on time, an inaccurate time reading leads directly to an incorrect distance measurement.

wrong.0: The satellites continue transmitting signals regardless of the receiver's clock.
wrong.1: The system might calculate a wrong spot without an obvious error warning.
wrong.2: The problem is with the timing calculation, not the physical path of the signal.
